ai_tweets.headline: China restricts OpenClaw at banks and government agencies — security concerns
ai_tweets.detail: Bloomberg and Reuters report Chinese government agencies and state-owned enterprises have warned staff against installing OpenClaw on office devices, citing security risks. This comes just days after Shenzhen announced OpenClaw development grants and Tencent shipped WorkBuddy.
ai_tweets.takeaway: Whiplash. Last week China was all-in (grants, product launches, stock surges). This week the security apparatus is pulling back. The pattern: companies move fast, regulators catch up. Not a ban — a restriction on government/SOE devices. Private sector adoption continues. Watch whether Tencent WorkBuddy is affected.

ai_tweets.headline: Meta acquires Moltbook — the social network where AI agents talk to each other
ai_tweets.detail: Meta acquired Moltbook, a Reddit-like social network built on OpenClaw where AI agents communicate with each other. The platform went viral partly due to AI-generated 'fake posts.' Deal expected to close mid-March. Confirmed by CNBC, TechCrunch, and AP News.
ai_tweets.takeaway: Meta is buying the agent social layer. If agents become a daily-use platform (like apps), the social network for agents becomes infrastructure. Meta sees this as the next social graph — not human-to-human, but agent-to-agent. Also notable: OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator in February. The talent war for agent infrastructure is real.

ai_tweets.headline: OpenClaw hits 250K+ GitHub stars — fastest-growing open-source project in history
ai_tweets.detail: CGTN reports OpenClaw surpassed 250,000 GitHub stars in under 4 months, a milestone that took Linux years to reach. Feature article covers the growth trajectory alongside the emerging security concerns around the agent ecosystem.
ai_tweets.takeaway: 250K stars in 4 months is unprecedented. For context: TensorFlow took 8 years to reach 185K. The growth validates the thesis that agents are a platform shift, not a feature. But the CGTN piece frames it as 'record growth + security panic' — the narrative is splitting between 'massive opportunity' and 'massive risk.'

ai_tweets.headline: AI agent supply chain attacks documented — OpenClaw skills ecosystem targeted
ai_tweets.detail: A practitioner's guide to AI agent security risks documents the 'OpenClaw malicious skills crisis' as the largest confirmed supply chain attack on AI agent infrastructure. Covers prompt injection, tool poisoning, and skill-level attacks.
ai_tweets.takeaway: The security story is real, not FUD. Supply chain attacks on skills are the new npm malware — but with agent-level permissions (file access, shell exec, network). If you install community skills without auditing, you're exposed. See Security Audit Tools skill above.

prompt_hack.title: The 'Provenance Gate' Pattern — Trust but Verify Agent-Installed Code
steps: Problem: Agents install skills, packages, and scripts — but most owners never audit what's running. Supply chain attacks on agents are now documented (see news above).

Add to AGENTS.md: 'Before installing any skill or package, check: (1) Is it certified on ClawHub? (2) Does the SKILL.md request elevated permissions or exec? (3) Does it write to paths outside the workspace?'
Create a pre-install checklist file: skills-audit-log.md. Log every skill installed with date, source, permissions requested, and audit status.
For high-risk skills (shell exec, network access, file writes outside workspace): read the SKILL.md and any scripts/ directory before installing. 5 minutes of review prevents supply chain compromise.
Pairs with the Security Audit Tools skill (edition #12) for automated scanning.
prompt_hack.why_it_matters: With 13,400+ skills on ClawHub and documented supply chain attacks, the 'install and hope' approach is over. A simple audit log and pre-install review adds minutes to your workflow but prevents the worst-case scenario: a compromised agent with access to your files, credentials, and shell.

model_radar.model: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B — Mixture of Experts, Runs Like a 3B
model_radar.detail: Qwen's MoE variant: 35B total parameters but only 3B active per inference. 1,073 likes and 1.35M downloads on HuggingFace — the most popular model this week by engagement. Multimodal (image-text-to-text).
model_radar.relevance: MoE changes the economics of local models. 35B quality at 3B inference cost means you can run frontier-adjacent reasoning on mid-range hardware. If you're using Qwen3.5-9B locally (like we are), this MoE variant might be the better choice — similar quality, potentially faster.

model_radar.detail: Fish Audio's latest TTS model trending on HuggingFace with 193 likes. Joins a growing wave of open-source speech models that agents can use for voice output without API costs.
model_radar.relevance: Voice output for agents is becoming commoditized. If your agent sends voice messages (Telegram, Discord), open-source TTS models eliminate per-message API costs. Fish Audio's quality has been competitive with commercial options.

community_build.title: The Agent Security Stack Is Forming — And It's Needed
community_build.description: This week marks a turning point: agent security went from theoretical to urgent. China restricting OpenClaw at government agencies, a documented supply chain attack on the skills ecosystem, MIT flagging no kill switches, and OpenAI shipping Codex Security. The community response is arriving too: Security Audit Tools and Inference Optimizer on ClawHub, the Provenance Gate pattern, and growing demand for skill certification. The question is no longer 'should agents be secured?' but 'who builds the security layer?' — and right now it's the community, not the platform.
community_build.how_to_replicate: Install Security Audit Tools. Add a pre-install audit step to your AGENTS.md. Review your cron jobs for over-permissioned tasks. Check which skills have shell exec access. Start an audit log. 30 minutes of security hygiene now prevents the headline later.
